meta.title: Corvus.Regex.Ecma262: the Industry benchmarks
meta.lede: Six engines over the Industry workloads of dotnet/performance: .NET's interpreter and source generator, this library's interpreter and source generator over UTF-16 and over UTF-8, and V8. Pick the engines to compare and the figure to compare them on; every view below follows.
facts: i7-13800H, WSL2, pinned to the P-cores
13.6 to 14.2 ns before, 13.2 to 14.2 ns after
meta.method:
Each figure is one Count over the whole text: every match found, as the benchmark of dotnet/performance measures it. The Corvus rows run under the u flag, which .NET has no mode for; counts agree on 53 of the 57 rows, and the four apart are $ and . at CRLF, where ECMA-262 counts CR as a line terminator, and \w, which .NET takes as Unicode letters and digits.

Where this library is slower, and why. Four kinds of row read above 1.0, each the price of an ECMA-262 rule .NET does not apply: . and $ at CRLF, where ECMA-262's . stops at CR as well as LF, so .* finds 36,491 matches to .NET's 26,105 at parity per match; case-insensitive patterns under the u flag, whose search must find the long s and the Kelvin sign as forms of s and k, which .NET's search ignores; a class that admits a supplementary character (two units) before a literal at a fixed distance, so the distance is not fixed ([a-q][^u-z]{13}x); and non-ASCII literals over UTF-8, where every Cyrillic or Chinese character is two or three bytes with no rare byte among them, against UTF-16's one rare unit per character. The other rows above 1.0 are within a few percent of parity and read either side of it from run to run.

The engines are .NET's interpreter (RegexOptions.None), .NET's source generator ([GeneratedRegex]), this library's interpreter over UTF-16, this library's source generator over UTF-16 and over UTF-8, and V8 (Node 24's RegExp, the oracle of the test data) over the same texts with the same flags as the Corvus rows, its matches counted by a test loop that advances lastIndex as matchAll does. The UTF-8 rows match the same text as bytes, with nothing transcoded.

The bar is the mean of BenchmarkDotNet's short job (one launch, three warm-ups, three iterations) and the whisker one standard deviation of its iterations; a row's ratio is read against its neighbours' rather than to the last few percent. Allocated is the bytes the benchmark allocated per operation; the library allocates nothing per match once its working memory has grown.

The host is WSL2 on Windows on an Intel Core i7-13800H, the VM pinned to the twelve performance cores (vmmemWSL affinity 0xFFF), the run under taskset -c 0-11 after a settle of at least three minutes, with a host probe at 13.6 to 14.2 ns before and 13.2 to 14.2 ns after (12.5 to 16 is the accepted band). .NET 10. Commit 535de98, 2026-10-20. The procedure is section 9 of the design document.
